title: Practice in messages
hookLine: write every message as if to a person, because it is

cards: A message with no greeting and no name: need this today. It was typed in a hurry, between two other things, and sent without a second look. On the other end, someone reads it standing at a kitchen counter.
Then reads it again. Are they in trouble? Is something wrong?
There's no face to check, no tone of voice, just the words, and the reader fills in the rest. Behind the screen name there's a person with a morning of their own. Today: Colossae.

teach.h: A SOFT ANSWER TURNETH AWAY WRATH.
teach.b: First, Proverbs, in the King James Bible: "A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger." Soft doesn't mean vague or weak. It means not grievous: not the word that wounds when a plainer one would do.
Second, a letter of Paul's, to the Christians at Colossae: "Let your speech be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man."
Grace and salt together: kind, but with some flavor in it. Honest, not syrup. Third, the Buddha.

In a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, he names five marks of speech that is well spoken: it's spoken at the right time, it's true, it's gentle, it's beneficial, and it's spoken with a mind of goodwill.
They fit a message almost too well. Is this the right time, or is it eleven at night? Is it true?
Is it gentle? Does it help? Is it written with goodwill, or with a sigh?
Fourth, why messages need this. Speech in a room comes with a face, a tone, a chance to fix a misunderstanding on the spot.
A message arrives bare, and the reader supplies the tone, sometimes harsher than the writer meant.
So the practice is small: write every message as if to a person, because it is. A greeting. A name.
A thank you. A when you have a moment. One word can be the difference between a soft answer and a grievous one.

how: Buddhists practice right speech, one part of the Noble Eightfold Path; Jews and Christians turn to Proverbs, and Christians also to the letters of Paul, for guidance on how to speak, and some apply the same teachings to writing.

games.q: it's late at night, and you've written a true, useful message to a colleague. the Buddha's five marks have another question for it. which?
games.why: well-spoken speech, he says, is spoken at the right time, as well as true, gentle, beneficial and with goodwill.

practice: Bring to mind one message you need to send, or one you sent recently, and picture the person reading it: where they are, what kind of day they might be having.
Read your words slowly, as they would, through the Buddha's five marks: the right time, true, gentle, helpful, written with goodwill.
Find one word to change or add, a greeting, their name, a thank you; if you pray, you can hold that person in your own tradition's words.
